extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in algebraic topology (readers learning homology and CW complexes)
extracted.subtask_description: Compute and reason about homology groups of CW complexes using cellular homology: degrees of attaching maps, cellular chain complexes, Mayer–Vietoris, Euler characteristic, and constructions (Moore spaces, lens spaces, projective spaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a map S^n→S^n via local degrees / preimages
rubrics_metrics.description: For almost all y∈S^n, f^{-1}(y) consists of points near which f is a local homeomorphism and the local degree at each preimage is ±1; by precomposing with reflections one may arrange local degrees to be ±1 as desired, so maps S^n→S^n of any integer degree can be produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute global degree by summing local degrees at preimages. Example: f(z)=z^k on S^1 has degree k because f^{-1}(y) has k points and each local degree = +1 (rotation homotopic to identity). Compose with reflection to change sign. For maps with isolated preimages, local-degree counting and local homeomorphism/ deformation arguments show local degree equals ±1 in many constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension preserves degree (Proposition 2.33)
rubrics_metrics.description: deg(Sf) = deg f where Sf : S^{n+1}→S^{n+1} is the suspension of f : S^n→S^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses cone and suspension pair long exact sequences and naturality of boundary maps; consequence: repeated suspension of z↦z^k gives maps of arbitrary degree in higher dimensions. Note: suspension maps only one point to each pole so local degree at each pole equals global degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2.34(a) — cellular relative homology basis correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a CW complex then H_k(X^n,X^{n-1}) is zero for k≠n and is free abelian for k=n, with a basis in one-to-one correspondence with the n-cells of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows because X^n/X^{n-1} is a wedge sum of n-spheres (one per n-cell); use Proposition 2.22/Corollary 2.25. Identification lets one think of elements of H_n(X^n,X^{n-1}) as linear combinations of n-cells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2.34(b) — vanishing above skeleton dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: H_k(X^n)=0 for k>n. In particular if X is finite-dimensional then H_k(X)=0 for k>dim X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from part (a) and examination of long exact sequences of the pairs (X^n,X^{n-1}). For infinite-dimensional complexes additional arguments (compactness of chains; mapping telescope) are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2.34(c) — inclusion-induced isomorphisms for lower dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The map H_k(X^n)→H_k(X) induced by inclusion X^n↪X is an isomorphism for k<n and surjective for k=n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from the long exact sequence of the pair (X^n,X^{n-1}) and the fact that singular chains meet only finitely many cells; for infinite-dimensional X a mapping-telescope reduction is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular chain complex and boundary maps (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using H_n(X^n,X^{n-1}) free with basis indexed by n-cells, define cellular chain groups and boundary maps d_n as compositions j_n ∂_{n+1} (relativizations of singular boundary maps); these satisfy d_n d_{n+1}=0, giving a chain complex called the cellular chain complex of X whose homology are the cellular homology groups H^{CW}_n(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagram-chasing in long exact sequences of adjacent skeleta shows compositions zero; think of chains as linear combinations of cells and the cellular boundary maps as encoding attaching map degrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 2.35 — cellular homology equals singular homology
rubrics_metrics.description: H^{CW}_n(X) ≅ H_n(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify H_n(X) with H_n(X^n)/Im ∂_{n+1} and use injectivity/isomorphism properties of inclusion-induced maps j_n to identify with Ker d_n/Im d_{n+1}. This justifies computing H_n(X) from the cellular chain complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications (i)–(iii) relating cells to homology
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) If X has no n-cells then H_n(X)=0. (ii) If X has k n-cells then H_n(X) is generated by at most k elements. (iii) If X has no two cells in adjacent dimensions then H_n(X) is free abelian with basis corresponding to n-cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These follow from the structure of the cellular chain complex: ranks/basis sizes controlled by number of cells and vanishing of boundary maps when no adjacent-dimension cells exist (so d_n automatically zero). Useful for quick homology deductions from CW-structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular boundary formula (degrees determine boundary coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-cell e^α_n with characteristic/attaching map ϕ_α:∂D^n_α→X^{n-1}, the cellular boundary d_n(e^α_n) = Σ_β d_{αβ} e^{β}_{n-1} where d_{αβ} is the degree of the composite ∂D^n_α→X^{n-1}→X^{n-1}/(X^{n-1} ackslash e^{β}_{n-1}) ≅ S^{n-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute d_{αβ} by collapsing complement of a target (n−1)-cell to a point and measuring degree of the resulting map S^{n-1}→S^{n-1}. Only finitely many terms appear since attaching maps have compact image. Use commutative diagrams of quotient maps and characteristic maps to derive formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientability detected by top homology (manifold criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed connected n-manifold M, H_n(M) ≅ Z if M is orientable and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies generally; shown later in Theorem 3.26 (referenced). Examples: orientable surfaces M_g give H_n=Z, nonorientable give 0 in top dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example criterion: nonorientable surface boundary map produces 2-torsion
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed nonorientable surface N_g with CW structure having one 2-cell attached by the word a_1^2 a_2^2 … a_g^2, the cellular boundary d_2(1) = (2, …, 2) so d_2 injective ⇒ H_2(N_g)=0 and H_1(N_g) ≅ Z^{g-1} ⊕ Z_2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute total exponent of each 1-cell in attaching word to get degrees (maps homotopic to z↦z^2). Changing bases can make torsion decomposition explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acyclic-but-noncontractible criterion via boundary matrix determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: If the cellular boundary matrix (e.g., d_2:Z^2→Z^2) is an isomorphism (determinant ±1), then all homology groups vanish (space is acyclic) though the space need not be contractible (π_1 may be nontrivial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: attaching two 2-cells to S^1∨S^1 by words whose abelianizations give matrix with determinant −1 yields H_i(X)=0 ∀i but π_1(X) has nontrivial finite quotients — homology does not detect contractibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local-degree computations for cellular boundaries in polyhedral identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When CW complexes are constructed from polyhedra with face identifications (e.g., tori, Klein bottle), local degrees on faces determine cellular boundary entries; reflections reverse sign (degree −1), rotations preserve sign (degree +1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For T^3 constructed from cube identifications, opposite faces contribute local degrees +1 and −1 which cancel, yielding d_3=0. For K×S^1 a rotation vs reflection changes signs and gives torsion in homology (e.g., Z⊕Z_2 summands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Moore spaces M(G,n) with prescribed homology
rubrics_metrics.description: Given abelian group G and n≥1, one can construct a CW complex X (a Moore space M(G,n)) with H_n(X) ≅ G and H_i(X)=0 for i≠n; if n>1 require M(G,n) simply-connected. Method: start with wedge of S^n's for generators of free part and attach (n+1)-cells with attaching maps of specified degrees to realize relations among generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finite cyclic summands Z_m, attach an (n+1)-cell by degree m map S^n→S^n. For general G, present G as F/K with F free, let attaching maps realize inclusions K↪F so the cellular boundary is K→F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary maps for RP^n (degree calculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: RP^n has one cell e^k in each k≤n and the attaching map for e^k is the 2-sheeted covering ϕ:S^{k-1}→RP^{k-1}; the composition qϕ has degree 1+(−1)^k, so d_k is either 0 (k odd) or multiplication by 2 (k even).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence the cellular chain complex alternates 0 and ×2 maps depending on parity, giving the standard homology of RP^n (Z in degree 0 and n when n odd, Z_2 in odd degrees < n, etc.). Compute degrees by comparing antipodal map degree (−1)^k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lens spaces cellular structure and alternating boundary maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite lens space L_m(ℓ_1,…,ℓ_n) admits a CW structure with one cell in each dimension ≤2n−1 and cellular boundary maps that alternate between 0 and multiplication by m; consequently H_k(L) = Z for k=0,2n−1; Z_m for odd k with 0<k<2n−1; and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by subdividing circle in last C-factor into m vertices and using balls joining vertices to S^{2n−3}, with identifications by rotation of order m; check degrees of face identifications (reflection gives −1, rotation +1) to derive alternating pattern. Infinite-dimensional lens spaces give Z_m in each odd dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler characteristic equals alternating sum of homology ranks (Theorem 2.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite CW complex X, χ(X)=Σ_n (−1)^n c_n (cells) and also χ(X)=Σ_n (−1)^n rank H_n(X), so Euler characteristic depends only on homotopy type and is independent of CW structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof is algebraic using chain complex decompositions Zn, Bn, Hn and rank additivity in short exact sequences. Useful to distinguish surfaces by χ (e.g., χ(M_g)=2−2g, χ(N_g)=2−g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting Lemma for short exact sequences and homology retract consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: For a short exact sequence 0→A→B→C→0 of abelian groups, the following are equivalent: (a) ∃p:B→A with p i = id_A; (b) ∃s:C→B with j s = id_C; (c) B ≅ A⊕C. If satisfied the sequence 'splits'. A retract r:X→A gives split short exact sequences 0→H_n(A)→H_n(X)→H_n(X,A)→0 and hence H_n(X) ≅ H_n(A)⊕H_n(X,A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use splitting to show nonexistence of retractions: e.g., no retraction D^n→S^{n−1} because it would force an impossible splitting in homology; mapping cylinder Mf of degree m>1 map does not retract to domain S^n since Z ≆ Z⊕Z_m. Over nonabelian groups only weaker semidirect product statements hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2.45 — torsion-freeness criterion for finite-dimensional K(G,1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a finite-dimensional CW complex X is a K(G,1), then G=π_1(X) must be torsionfree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If G had torsion (a subgroup Z_m), the corresponding covering space would be a finite-dimensional K(Z_m,1) whose homology would have Z_m in infinitely many dimensions, contradicting finite-dimensionality. Use known H_n(Z_m) ≠ 0 for infinitely many n from lens-space calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayer–Vietoris sequence (long exact sequence and boundary map construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For subspaces A,B⊂X with X the union of interiors of A and B, there is a long exact Mayer–Vietoris sequence …→H_n(A∩B)→H_n(A)⊕H_n(B)→H_n(X)→H_{n−1}(A∩B)→… ; the sequence arises from the short exact sequence of chain complexes 0→C_n(A∩B)→C_n(A)⊕C_n(B)→C_n(A+B)→0 with explicit maps ϕ(x)=(x,−x), ψ(x,y)=x+y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compute boundary ∂:H_n(X)→H_{n−1}(A∩B) represent α∈H_n(X) by a cycle z and write z = x+y with x∈C_n(A), y∈C_n(B); then ∂α is represented by ∂x = −∂y in H_{n−1}(A∩B). Applications: S^n as union of hemispheres recovers H_n(S^n); Klein bottle decomposition A∪B yields explicit map Z→Z⊕Z (1↦(2,−2)) producing H_2=0 and H_1=Z⊕Z_2. Mayer–Vietoris also applies when A,B are deformation retracts of neighborhoods.
